cues.text: A Priest's Private Doubt
In 1263, the Bohemian priest Peter of Prague was traveling to Rome on pilgrimage.
He stopped in the lakeside town of Bolsena and was given permission to celebrate Mass at the tomb of the young martyr St. Christina in the town's basilica.

Though outwardly a devout and dutiful priest, he had for some time struggled privately with doubt over whether the bread he consecrated at every Mass truly underwent transubstantiation into the Body of Christ.
Blood at the Consecration
As he spoke the words of consecration, tradition holds, blood began to seep visibly from the Host, running over his hands and down onto the corporal, the linen cloth spread beneath the chalice.

Startled and ashamed, Peter is said to have first tried to conceal what had happened before abandoning the attempt and, unable to continue the Mass, setting out at once for nearby Orvieto, where Pope Urban IV was then residing.
An Investigation, and a Pope's Judgment
Urban IV heard the priest's account, granted him absolution, and dispatched emissaries to examine the corporal and question witnesses at Bolsena.
Satisfied that no natural explanation accounted for what had occurred, the pope ordered the diocesan bishop to bring the stained Host and linen to Orvieto.
There, he received them personally in a solemn procession attended by cardinals and prelates of his court.
A Feast for the Whole Church
The Bolsena miracle is widely credited, alongside broader currents of thirteenth-century Eucharistic devotion, with confirming Urban IV in his intention.
He sought to establish a feast honoring Christ's presence in the Eucharist for the universal Church.
On August 11, 1264, he issued the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo , instituting the Solemnity of Corpus Christi.
He commissioned St. Thomas Aquinas to compose its liturgical texts, including the hymns Pange Lingua and Tantum Ergo still sung at its celebration today.

Some of Urban's own contemporary biographers, notably, make no mention of the Bolsena episode at all in recounting his reasons for the feast, a silence historians have weighed carefully against the far more widely repeated devotional account.
Enshrined at Orvieto
The blood-stained corporal remains enshrined today in the Cathedral of Orvieto, in a dedicated Chapel of the Corporal.
Built in the mid-fourteenth century to house it, the chapel’s walls are covered in frescoes depicting the episodes of the miracle.
The Renaissance master Raphael would later paint his own celebrated version of the scene, The Mass at Bolsena , for the papal apartments in the Vatican.
Legacy

Every year, Orvieto and towns throughout the Catholic world mark the anniversary with processions of the Blessed Sacrament, the same feast Urban IV's bull first established seven and a half centuries ago.
Growing from a single priest's confessed doubt in a small lakeside church, it became one of the most widely celebrated solemnities on the Catholic calendar.
In the memory of the Church, it joins earlier reported Eucharistic signs of that same turbulent century at Florence and Daroca .
A full five centuries after Lanciano , it echoes the same pattern the Church has returned to again and again: a sincere doubt met not with condemnation.
It was met instead with a sign that drew the whole Church's worship of the Eucharist out into open, public procession.
